GHSA-q7v9-x93c-xqv3.summary: zip: Unbounded Symlink-Target Handling Can Abort Or Exhaust Memory During Extraction
GHSA-q7v9-x93c-xqv3.details:
### Summary

The symbolic-link branch of `ZipArchive::extract_internal()` allocates a buffer using an attacker-declared size before reading any entry data. A 112-byte archive terminates the extracting process with `SIGABRT` through this infallible allocation.

### Details

```rust
#[cfg(any(unix, windows))]
if file.is_symlink() {
    let mut target = Vec::with_capacity(file.size() as usize); // @audit unbounded memory allocation
    file.read_to_end(&mut target)?;
    drop(file);
    make_symlink(&outpath, &target, &self.shared.files)?;
    continue;
}
```

[`src/read/mod.rs#L399-L405`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/mod.rs#L399-L405) (reviewed commit `6f09b306`); the same code is at [`src/read.rs#L417-L418`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/v8.6.0/src/read.rs#L417-L418) in released v8.6.0.

Both inputs are attacker-controlled:

- [`ZipFile::size()`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/zipfile.rs#L243-L246) returns `uncompressed_size` verbatim from the central directory record. A ZIP64 extended-information extra field widens it to a full `u64` ([`src/read/mod.rs#L619-L625`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/mod.rs#L619-L625)). It is never cross-checked against the compressed size, the remaining archive length, or any platform-appropriate bound for a symlink target.
- [`ZipFile::is_symlink()`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/zipfile.rs#L256-L260) is decided entirely by the central directory's external-attributes field, via the `S_IFLNK` bit.

**Memory allocation failure → uncatchable process abort.** The reservation is sized from the declared `uncompressed_size` before a single byte of the entry is read. `Vec::with_capacity()` is infallible: on allocator refusal it calls `handle_alloc_error()`, which aborts the process. This is not a Rust panic — it is not caught by `catch_unwind()`, is unaffected by `panic = "unwind"`, and is not contained by isolating the call in a worker thread. This was verified by wrapping the call in all three at once; the process still died with exit 134.

The declared value needed is a property of the host's address space, not of reachability. On a 64 GB host with heuristic overcommit, declared sizes from roughly `2^38` upward abort reliably. Sizes at or above `2^63` instead trip `Vec`'s internal capacity check and produce a *catchable* `capacity overflow` panic, so an attacker simply avoids that band. The reproducer declares `2^62`, which exceeds the 47-bit user address space of x86-64 Linux outright and therefore aborts deterministically regardless of installed RAM or overcommit policy. Under a `ulimit -v` cap or a memory-constrained container the threshold drops far enough that a plain 32-bit `uncompressed_size` with no ZIP64 field suffices — a virtual-memory limit lowers the bar rather than mitigating the defect.

This is process termination, not memory exhaustion: `Vec::with_capacity()` only maps address space and never touches pages, so resident memory stays flat and the abort happens on the refused reservation itself, before any byte is read.

### PoC

The reproducer consists of the following `zip` harness and payload. It requires only the `zip` crate; use a standard Base64 decoder to materialise the archive before running it.

```toml
[package]
name = "zip-poc"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
zip = "8.6.0"
```

```rust
use std::{env, fs::File, io::BufReader};

fn main() {
    let archive_path = env::args().nth(1).expect("usage: poc <archive.zip>");
    let outdir = std::env::temp_dir().join("zip-poc");
    std::fs::create_dir_all(&outdir).unwrap();

    let file = File::open(archive_path).unwrap();
    let mut archive = zip::ZipArchive::new(BufReader::new(file)).unwrap();
    let r = archive.extract(&outdir);            // <-- process dies here
    println!("SURVIVED: {:?}", r);
}
```

Save the Base64 payload below as `archive.b64`, remove its whitespace, decode it with a standard Base64 decoder (for example, `base64 -d archive.b64 > archive.zip` on Linux), and run `cargo run --release -- archive.zip`.

**Uncatchable abort — 112 bytes.** One `Stored` entry named `a`; external attributes `0xA1FF0000` (`S_IFLNK|0777`); ZIP64 extra field declaring `uncompressed_size = 2^62`; zero-byte payload. sha256 `0c68c3934f22651a6bd2726f7d58140124b1839196a1d0ae468864cdfda74676`.

```
UEsDBC0AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAP////8BAAAAYVBLAQItAy0AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAP//
//8BAAwAAAAAAAAAAAD/oQAAAABhAQAIAAAAAAAAAABAUEsFBgAAAAABAAEAOwAAAB8AAAAAAA==
```

Observed on x86-64 Linux, rustc 1.93.1, release profile, against both the reviewed commit and released v8.6.0:

```
entries=1
memory allocation of 4611686018427387904 bytes failed
Aborted (core dumped)          # exit 134
```

The `SURVIVED` line never prints. Wrapping `extract()` in `catch_unwind` inside a spawned thread with `panic = "unwind"` produces the identical outcome.

### Impact

Applications running on Unix or Windows targets that call `ZipArchive::extract()` on attacker-supplied input are affected, with default features and no special configuration. The malicious 112-byte archive causes an unrecoverable, uncatchable termination of the extracting process, repeatable at will and not mitigable at the call site with `catch_unwind`, a worker thread, or a pre-flight metadata check.

Upload handling, mail-attachment processing, package and artefact ingestion, backup restore and container-image layer extraction all match this pattern. No confidentiality or integrity property is affected: no memory unsafety, no out-of-bounds access, no disclosure and no data corruption.

### Suggested remediation

Before allocating, compare `file.size()` with a documented, platform-appropriate maximum symlink-target length and reject entries that exceed it. Alternatively, replace `Vec::with_capacity()` with fallible `try_reserve()` and return an I/O error when allocation fails. Do not use Linux's `PATH_MAX` as a cross-platform contract.

Apply the allocation fix to `src/read/stream.rs` as defence-in-depth, although its symlink path is currently unreachable because streaming entries have no symlink attributes.

For reference, the crate already applies exactly this defence to another untrusted size on the same path: `ZipArchive::new()` clamps a suspicious `number_of_files` to zero and explicitly rejects an oversized central directory before reserving ([`src/read/zip_archive.rs#L185-L202`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/zip_archive.rs#L185-L202)). The symlink branch received neither guard. A survey of `Vec::with_capacity` across `src/` finds exactly two sites sized from untrusted input: `src/read/mod.rs:401` and `src/read/stream.rs:73`.

RUSTSEC-2026-0194.summary: Quadratic run time when checking a start tag for duplicate attribute names
RUSTSEC-2026-0194.details:
`BytesStart::attributes()` returns an `Attributes` iterator which, by default
(`with_checks(true)`), rejects a start tag that repeats an attribute name. For
each attribute yielded, the iterator compared the new name against every name
seen so far in the same tag using a linear scan, so a start tag with `N`
distinct attribute names cost `O(N²)` byte comparisons. There was no bound on
`N` other than the size of the buffered start tag.

## Impact

Any code that parses untrusted XML and iterates a start tag's attributes with
the default duplicate check enabled can be made to spend CPU time quadratic in
the number of attributes on a single tag. Because the check is pure computation
with no `.await`/I/O, an I/O-based timeout on the consumer (for example a read
or request timeout) cannot interrupt it while it runs.

Measured cost of a single start tag, release build:

| Attributes on one tag | Time |
|---|---|
| 80,000  | ~6 s   |
| 800,000 | ~10 min |

The cost grows with the square of the attribute count, so a start tag of a few
tens of megabytes can stall a parsing thread for hours. No memory is exhausted
and the parser does not crash; the effect is CPU exhaustion on the thread doing
the parsing: a single crafted start tag can pin a CPU core for minutes to hours,
denying service to that worker. A deployment that places a wall-clock bound on
parsing, or confines it to a non-critical thread, may consider the availability
impact lower.

## Affected code paths

* `BytesStart::attributes()` / `Attributes` iterated with checks enabled (the
  default), and `BytesStart::try_get_attribute`.
* `NsReader`, which resolves namespaces by iterating a tag's attributes and so
  reaches the same check internally.

Consumers that iterate attributes with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` and do
not use `NsReader` are not affected.

This was reported as reachable by a remote, unauthenticated attacker in a
real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet Labs Routinator) via a crafted RRDP
`snapshot.xml`.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`, where the duplicate check keeps the linear
scan for start tags with a small number of attributes and switches to an `O(1)`
hash pre-filter above a threshold, making the whole tag `O(N)`. The reported
`AttrError::Duplicated` positions are unchanged.

If upgrading is not possible and duplicate-name detection is not required,
disable it with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` (this does not help
`NsReader` consumers, which have no equivalent opt-out before 0.41.0).

RUSTSEC-2026-0195.summary: Unbounded namespace-declaration allocation in `NsReader` enables memory-exhaustion denial of service
RUSTSEC-2026-0195.details:
`NsReader` resolves namespaces by calling `NamespaceResolver::push` for every
`Start`/`Empty` event *before* the event is returned to the caller. `push`
iterated all `xmlns` / `xmlns:*` attributes on the start tag and, for each one,
appended the prefix bytes to an internal buffer and pushed a `NamespaceBinding`
(32 bytes on 64-bit) to an internal `Vec`, with no upper bound on the number of
declarations.

## Impact

A start tag with `N` namespace declarations drove roughly `3×` the tag's byte
size in `NamespaceResolver` heap, allocated *inside* `quick-xml` before the
`NsReader` consumer ever received the event and could inspect or reject it. A
consumer that bounds its *input* size therefore still cannot bound this
allocation: an `M`-byte start tag yields on the order of `3 × M` bytes of
resolver heap the caller never sees.

On untrusted XML this lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker force large heap
allocations with a single start tag. With several `NsReader`s running
concurrently on independent inputs (a common server pattern), the allocations
stack and can exhaust process memory, causing the operating system to kill the
process (OOM). This was confirmed against a real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet
Labs Routinator), where concurrent RRDP validation workers parsing a crafted
`snapshot.xml` exceeded the memory limit and the process was OOM-killed.

## Affected code paths

Consumers using `NsReader` (which always calls `NamespaceResolver::push` before
yielding `Start`/`Empty`), or calling `NamespaceResolver::push` directly. A plain
`Reader` that does not perform namespace resolution is not affected.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`. `NamespaceResolver::push` now rejects a start
tag that declares more than `DEFAULT_MAX_DECLARATIONS_PER_ELEMENT` (256)
namespace bindings, returning the new `NamespaceError::TooManyDeclarations`
instead of allocating without limit. The limit is configurable via
`NamespaceResolver::set_max_declarations_per_element` (use `usize::MAX` to
restore the previous unbounded behavior), and `NsReader::resolver_mut()` is
provided to reach it.

There is no clean workaround for `NsReader` consumers before 0.41.0, as the
allocation happens inside the reader with no configuration knob to cap it.

RUSTSEC-2026-0367.summary: Insecure Preservation of SUID/SGID Bits during ZIP Extraction Leading to Potential Privilege Escalation
RUSTSEC-2026-0367.details:
The `zip` crate preserves privileged Unix permission bits (SUID, SGID, and sticky bits) from ZIP `external_attributes` during extraction, instead of masking them to safe permission bits. If a privileged process (for example, `root` in an installer, CI/CD pipeline, or container build) extracts an attacker-controlled ZIP archive using `ZipArchive::extract()` or the stream extraction API, files can be created as setuid-root or setgid. This behavior allows the creation of SUID/SGID files during extraction, which can lead to local privilege escalation depending on the execution environment.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-vv5m-jxxh-4627

RUSTSEC-2026-0368.summary: zip: `ZipArchive::extract` creates symbolic links whose attacker-controlled targets are outside the destination directory
RUSTSEC-2026-0368.details:
In `zip` 9.0.0-pre2, `ZipArchive::extract` creates a symbolic link from an archive entry after validating only the output entry path. The link target bytes are passed directly to the platform symlink API, so a malicious archive can create an entry inside the destination that resolves to an attacker-chosen path outside it. This behavior was verified on macOS and Linux. On either platform, a subsequent application read or write through that extracted entry accesses the external target with the extracting process's permissions.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4v9h-p7m9-rh26

RUSTSEC-2026-0369.summary: ZipStreamReader::extract() and ZipArchive::extract() apply Unix permissions through symlinks without confining the target
RUSTSEC-2026-0369.details:
`ZipStreamReader::extract()` applies Unix permissions through extracted symlinks without validating the symlink target stays within the destination

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4684-h2q9-2vcp
